summary: Recommends how independent operators, such as enterprises and ISPs, should run email submission and transport services. The aim is clearer accountability so abuse like spam and worms is easier to control. It is a Best Current Practice document.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail from strangers should come with a name tag. This recommends how mail providers should check who is sending so that spammers cannot hide.

questions: how to reduce spam from email submission
what is the email submission port
what is a mail submission agent
subtitle: Operational rules that make the first hop of email, from a user's mail program to a mail server, accountable.

tldr.problem: Email passes between independent operators with no prior arrangement, so it is hard to debug problems or assign accountability when spam or worms are injected into the mail system.
tldr.mechanism: Operators run message submission on port 587, require authentication and authorization for every submission, keep submissions traceable to the authenticated user, and never act as open relays.
tldr.outcome: These policies do not solve spam on their own, but they clarify lines of accountability between operators. The RFC is a Best Current Practice and has since been updated by RFC 8314.

facts.label: Traceability note
facts.value: Transit issues often occur up to one week after submission

today: RFC 5068 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 134) and has been updated by RFC 8314. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Submission Needs Rules
sections.content:
Email is convenient because it is nearly everywhere, fast, cheap and works without prior arrangement. Those same traits make it a fertile ground for spam, fraud and worms. On its way to the recipient, a message often crosses several independent providers that have no arrangement with one another, which makes problems hard to debug and accountability hard to assign.

Many email authentication technologies exist, but submission, the first step from a Mail User Agent (MUA) to a Mail Submission Agent (MSA), is the weakest link. Without strong practices there, authentication elsewhere in the service has limited benefit. The RFC covers only submission; relaying and delivery are out of scope.

The policies can be adopted by operators of any size, independently, whether or not the other side of an email exchange has adopted them. The RFC states plainly that adopting them alone will not solve spam.
sections.plainLanguage: The first step of sending mail, handing it to your mail server, is where cheating is easiest. This RFC says to guard that first door well.

sections.title: The Four Mail Components
sections.content:
Internet email has four message-handling components: Mail User Agents (MUAs), Mail Submission Agents (MSAs), Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) and Mail Delivery Agents (MDAs).

An MUA works for the user to create a message and submit it through an MSA. The MSA accepts it, does any needed preprocessing, and relays it to an MTA. MTAs relay messages onward in a sequence until a destination MDA delivers it to the recipient's inbox. These parts are often combined in one piece of software, but the RFC notes that separating them is increasingly common.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a postal chain: you hand a letter to the local post office, trucks carry it along, and a mail carrier drops it in the right mailbox.

sections.title: Submission, Relaying and Delivery
sections.content:
Originally the submission, relay and delivery roles were seen as one unit, and all of them used SMTP over TCP port 25. Mail can be exchanged on port 25 without prior arrangement and without sender authentication, so relaying MTAs may not know who the originator really is.

The RFC asks readers to separate three steps: MUA-to-MSA submission, MTA relaying, and the final MTA-to-MDA handoff. Submission typically involves an existing relationship between the user and the server operator, and the MDA knows its recipients. An MSA can therefore reject postings from MUAs it has no relationship with, and an MDA can reject mail for recipients it does not serve. Both policies are already in common practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Your own post office knows you, and the final mail carrier knows the neighbors. Only the middle of the journey deals with strangers, so the two ends can be strict.

sections.title: Best Practices for Submission Operation
sections.content:
The RFC lists five practices:

  • Port availability: if external submissions are supported, the domain's MSAs MUST support the submission port 587. Operators MAY use it for local users too.
  • Port use: MUAs SHOULD use port 587 for submission.
  • Authentication: MSAs MUST authenticate the identity asserted in all mail transactions on that port, even when the recipient would not be relayed outside the local domain.
  • Authorization: the operator MUST ensure the authenticated identity is authorized to submit, based on an existing relationship.
  • Accountability: for a reasonable period, the message SHOULD be traceable to the authenticated user. The RFC leaves the length open but notes that transit issues often occur as much as one week after submission.

To move submission off port 25, MSAs MUST listen on port 587 by default, SHOULD be able to listen on other ports, and MUST require authentication on port 587. Whatever port is used, MSAs MUST NOT relay unauthenticated messages to other domains, that is, they must not be open relays. MUAs SHOULD try the best submission port from a list with 587 first.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the special front door for sending mail, show your ID every time, and the post office must be able to remember who sent each letter for a while.

sections.title: External Submission
sections.content:
An MUA may need to submit mail across the Internet to its home MSA rather than to a local one, for example to get privacy protection against monitoring, including by the operator of its access network. That makes the access provider an involuntary participant in fighting mass-effect email problems.

Some providers block outbound port 25 or redirect it to a local SMTP proxy except for authorized hosts. This can hurt legitimate mobile users trying to reach their home MSA. The RFC makes no recommendation about blocking port 25. It instead promotes the official submission port 587.

Two practices follow. Access providers MUST NOT block users from reaching the external Internet on port 587. And email service providers MUST distinguish unauthenticated mail addressed to local domains (MX traffic) from authenticated submission mail that can be addressed anywhere (MSA traffic), so that relaying can be restricted and open relays prevented. Secondary MXs and similar internal setups may be exceptions.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are away from home, like at a coffee shop, you should still be able to use the special front door to your own post office, and nobody on the way should lock it.

sections.title: Authentication Technologies
sections.content:
The RFC does not pick a mechanism. It names two standardized building blocks, SMTP AUTH (RFC 4954) and TLS for SMTP (RFC 3207), and says that different environments suit different mechanisms, sometimes in combination. Organizations SHOULD choose the most secure approaches that are practical.

It does warn that sending user credentials in clear text over insecure networks SHOULD be avoided in all scenarios, because attackers could listen and steal account data.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to show your ID. Pick a safe one, and never shout your password across a crowded room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is short. Email transfer between independent administrations can be the source of large volumes of unwanted email and of messages containing malicious content meant to attack the recipient's system. The document describes requirements and procedures that permit such exchanges while reducing the likelihood that malicious mail is transmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting strangers exchange mail is useful but risky, so these rules make bad mail a little harder to send.

items.title: Port 587
items.text: MSAs must support the submission port if they accept external submissions.

items.title: Authenticate
items.text: Every transaction on the submission port is authenticated.

items.title: Authorize
items.text: The authenticated identity must be allowed to submit.

items.title: Trace
items.text: Keep the message traceable to the user for a reasonable time.

items.title: No open relay
items.text: Never relay unauthenticated messages to other domains.
